ENT Clinical Note

Subjective:
- Presenting complaint and trigger/exposure: Progressive shortness of breath and “tightness” noted over the last 2–3 days, first noticed while running; no clear food, medication, or environmental trigger identified.
- Symptom timeline and progression: Symptoms began 2–3 days ago; now occur with brisk walking. Salbutamol (“blue inhaler”) provides no relief.
- ENT symptoms:
  • Throat swelling/closure sensation: Denied  
  • Voice change/hoarseness: Denied  
  • Dysphagia/odynophagia, drooling: Denied  
  • Nasal/ocular: Seasonal allergic rhinitis (“hay fever”)  
  • Stridor/noisy breathing: Denied; reports wheeze only  
  • Dyspnea: Present, exertional and now at rest with conversation  
  • Facial/lip/tongue/uvular swelling: Denied  
  • Ear/neck symptoms: None
- Relevant past episodes and treatments: Last asthma “attack” 3–4 years ago; no prior hospital admission or oral steroid/antibiotic therapy. No prior adrenaline/epinephrine use.
- Allergies and current medications:
  • Drug/food allergies: None reported  
  • Current medications:  
    – Salbutamol inhaler (dose/route/frequency not documented; patient using PRN)  
    – Clenil (beclomethasone) inhaler 3 puffs BID (patient-directed increase to 4 puffs BID advised)  
    – Cetraben topical emollient (dose/route/frequency not documented)  
    – Hydrocortisone topical (dose/route/frequency not documented)
- Social context: Attending tele-consultation alone from private residence.

Objective:
- Observable swelling: None reported/visualized.
- Airway/breathing: Patient reports wheeze; no stridor heard over video. Work of breathing not documented.
- Mental status: Alert, conversational.
- Vitals and physical examination: Not recorded.
- Accompaniment: None.

Assessment:
- Likely mild asthma exacerbation (upper-airway involvement not evident). Justification: onset 2–3 days, exercise-induced dyspnea, wheeze, inadequate response to reliever inhaler, no signs of anaphylaxis or angio-edema.

Plan:
- Increase preventer (Clenil) to 4 puffs BID while awaiting review.
- Salbutamol inhaler may be used up to every 2 hours PRN; if this frequency is required, symptoms worsen, or breathing deteriorates, patient to attend Emergency Department immediately.
- Book face-to-face GP/respiratory review within the next few days for examination, peak-flow measurement, and consideration of oral steroids ± antibiotics.
- Red-flag advice: seek emergency care for increasing breathlessness, inability to speak full sentences, nocturnal awakening, chest tightness not relieved by inhaler, or any new throat tightness, voice change, or facial/tongue swelling.
- Education: Confirm correct inhaler technique and adherence at upcoming visit; continue allergen avoidance measures for hay fever.

Quality checks (document_quality):
• Missing but expected: Objective vital signs, auscultation findings, peak-flow measurement, detailed inhaler doses, prior written asthma/ENT action plan, availability of spacer or auto-injector (not applicable but usually queried).  
• Internal conflicts: None noted.  
• Transcript quality: Clear; occasional overlaps/inaudible drug names (“Flanel/Bactroban”) but did not alter clinical content.
